utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone. Today, we are holding a status conference to address a number of matters and ensure that we are on track for the resumption of the trial hearings on 1st of March. First, can I please have the appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. Alan Tieger, Hildegard Uertz-Retzlaff, and Iain Reid for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Mr. Karadzic, I see that you again are here alone, and I take it that you are continuing to represent yourself.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not totally on my own. There's always someone with me in spirit. But I shall defend myself, by myself, until the end of these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. On 19th November, 2009, the Registrar appointed Mr. Richard Harvey to prepare for the resumption of the trial on 1st of March, 2010, in case it should become necessary for him to represent the interests of the accused at that time, following our decision of 5th of November, 2009. The Registrar's appointment of Mr. Harvey is currently the subject of an appeal by Mr. Karadzic. In light of this fact, Mr. Harvey was reluctant to be present in the courtroom at today's status conference without the consent of Mr. Karadzic. As Mr. Karadzic has objected to his presence, it is my understanding then Mr. Harvey is following these proceedings from the public gallery. While Mr. Harvey's role in the trial proceedings, if any, remains to be determined, the Chamber trusts that he is continuing his vigorous preparations for the trial in case it should become necessary for him to represent the interests of the accused. Should he be experiencing any difficulties with his preparations which he considers it necessary to bring to our attention, the Chamber will accept any written submissions on this matter that he wishes to make. I would like now to go through the items on today's agenda. The first item relates to the pending several binding-order motions filed by Mr. Karadzic. As you are aware, Mr. Karadzic, there have been a number of steps taken by the Chamber to encourage the states from which you have requested material to provide that material to you on a voluntary basis. Some progress has thus been made, and you have withdrawn several of your motions. However, there remain a number of them still pending. In order to move things along on this, the Chamber will hold a motions hearing on Monday, 15th of February, to which representatives of the relevant states will be invited. We therefore need to compile a list of states to be invited to attend this hearing, and to this end I would like to go through some of your remaining pending motions and ask some further questions. The first motion relates to your motion for binding order against the Government of Germany, filed on 13th August 2009. In a written submission filed on 25th of September last year, Germany disputed the relevance of most of the categories of documents sought by the accused, and agreed to search for one category of documents. I would simply note that this motion remains pending, and the resolution of the matter is not expected through the parties' negotiation on a voluntary basis, except for the resolution by the Chamber. Therefore, the Chamber will hold a hearing on this, after which the decision on the motion will be issued. The motion hearings on this will take place at 9.00 on 15th of February, 2010, to which, of course, the representative of Germany will, of course, be invited. I turn to your next motion for binding order, i.e., against Italy, which was filed on 4th of August, 2009. Very recently, the day before yesterday, i.e., that is, on 26th of January, Italy filed correspondence on a confidential basis, attaching a number of documents. The Chamber notes Italy's indication that the documents have been provided on a confidential basis and may not be disclosed without its permission, which would include any public disclosure, though used at trial. So, Mr. Karadzic, I take it that you understand and recognise these conditions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, absolutely. I am grateful for all the government co-operation received so far. Italy provided quite a few articles from different publications. So far, this is the first time we are getting something substantial. So from that point of view, I wish to assure you that the Defence is not going to violate Rule 70 in any way. We hope, of course, that other documents will be received from Italy, too. We believe that this is not all. This has been submitted for a translation, and I'm afraid that at one point in time translation is going to become a bottleneck in these proceedings. So we have to be aware of that, that there is going to be a great deal of material to be translated, and perhaps it won't be done in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So that triggers my second question to you, which is whether, as a result of reviewing the documents, whether you are in a position to state whether you will withdraw your motion or whether you think it is necessary to hear from Italy at the binding-order motions hearing, following which of course the Chamber can issue its decision on the motion.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I received that in the Italian language, which unfortunately I do not speak. I do not know any Italian, so I have to wait for the translation to see whether that is everything that we had expected. If you allow me to do so, I will respond within a week's time, or, rather, as soon as I receive the translation I will say whether we can withdraw that or whether we should kindly ask the representative of Italy to be present here on the 15th of February.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could let us know your position as soon as possible. Next item relates to your motion against France, filed on 24th of August last year. On 7th December last year, a confidential letter from France was filed, attaching a document in response to the accused's request. We note that you have indicated that, in principle, you do not oppose the protective measures requested by France. Therefore, likewise, the Chamber wishes to clarify whether it is your position that the provisions of Rule 70 apply to the document you have received from France.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, that applies to France as well. I do appreciate the fact that this one document came in, but I believe that France has a great many more documents, since the French military and political presence in the Balkans, especially in Bosnia, was massive. I'm convinced that France can help us a great deal. As for Rule 70, of course, it applies to each and every country, France included. The Defence is not going to reveal any confidential documents to anyone. If we do not receive anything else by the 15th, and I am convinced that France has significant documents and knowledge about developments and the essence of the crisis in Bosnia-Herzegovina, then we would be pleased to see here the representatives of France on the 15th of February as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So in order to clarify this matter, I wonder whether you have received any other responses from France to your follow-up request.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I received that one document, along with the letter, and I wrote again on the 7th of January, and I provided them with some specific information concerning the documents that we need, that the Defence needs. However, so far I have not received a response to that letter. We are expecting that. I did that because I thought it would be right to try to reach an agreement before a decision is made by the Trial Chamber. So the letter went on the 7th of January, and we hope that we will get a response and it does provide localities and other specific information concerning documents that we're interested in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: To wrap it up, when do you think you are in the position to tell us whether, in your opinion, it is necessary to hear from France at the binding-order motions hearing?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the moment when I receive yet another reply from them. If it is an exhaustive reply and if we receive all the documents that we believe and know the French government has, at that moment I can state my views. The Defence will promptly state its views to the Trial Chamber. However, if we do not receive that, and if there is a significant amount of documents that are not being sent in, then we would like to see a representative of France here. Believe me, France is one of the most important countries in this crisis. They gave a major contribution to peace, and their representatives in the civilian sector and their military officers rendered a major contribution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you, by any chance, know by when the French government will respond to your request?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no indication whatsoever. I know that I sent my letter on the 7th of January. I do not have any response. I haven't had one over these past three weeks. I have no indication as to when they're going to reply. Perhaps, in a way, this could be an encouragement. A public appeal to the French government to act in that direction, that would be a good thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then I will turn to the next motion against Bosnia, which was filed on 1st of September, 2009. Again, my question for you, Mr. Karadzic, is whether you have received a response from Bosnia to your follow-up request, and what your position is with regard to the documentation that you have received from Bosnia. Is there any change from the information you provided in your memorandum of 8th of January?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the 7th of January, I received six documents that are rather useful. However, they are just a tiny part of what we need from Bosnia-Herzegovina, from the government documents there. I repeated my request of the 7th of January, as I did in the case of France. There are going to be a few more significant requests addressed to the Bosnian government. They had investigations carried out in respect of their own units and their own criminals, and that caused certain behaviour on our part in Sarajevo. So without that, the proceedings would not be fair. Therefore, we are expecting to hear from them so that we could submit new requests to Bosnia. What is encourage is a statement made by Samo Siketic, the minister of defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that I will receive everything I'm asking for from Bosnia-Herzegovina. However, things are moving rather slowly. If we do not receive anything by the 7th of February, for instance, it would be a good thing if not only a representative of Bosnia-Herzegovina would be here on the 15th of February, but also a representative of the OHR, the Office of the High Representative in Bosnia-Herzegovina, who has the power and authority to persuade each and every institution in Bosnia-Herzegovina to co-operate with this Tribunal. We will, indeed, have to wait for quite a few documents coming in from them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My next question is about Croatia, the motion about which was filed on the 11th of September, 2009. Once again, I would like to know whether you have received a response from the Croatian government to your follow-up letter of 7th of January, and what your position is with regard to the documentation you have received from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for these 15 documents that I received from Croatia, they are, indeed, useful. However, they only represent a tiny part of what Croatia can provide us with. I haven't received any response from Croatia yet, either, to my letter of the 7th of January. However, they had elections held in their country, there is a new president, and I understand that this was not a priority of theirs. At any rate, it would be a good thing if a representative of the Croatian government would be here on the 15th of February as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My next question is regarding the Government of Netherlands. The motion was filed on the 11th of September, 2009, and it seems to me that there are two remaining documents which the Netherlands has indicated it is trying to locate. Do you have any update on this, and do you wish to withdraw your motion in light of the material that you have received, as you did in relation to the United States?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm very grateful to the Dutch government for these nine documents and for the efforts made to find these additional two documents. If this does happen and if they can be encouraged to that effect, namely, that we receive these documents, it would not be indispensable to have them present here on the 15th of February. At the moment I would receive these two additional documents, I would withdraw my motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I have to correct myself, that you didn't withdraw your motion with respect to the United States; instead, that your motion was denied without prejudice. Yes. Next question is about Iran, the motion about which was filed on 26th of August, 2009. The Chamber has granted an extension of the dead-line for Iran to respond to the motion, and that dead-line expires tomorrow. So unless you have anything further to say on this, Mr. Karadzic, I think we will have to wait for Iran's response before deciding what further action to take on this one. Do you have anything to say, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I do expect Iran to provide this to us. So far, we have established that the USA encouraged Iran to violate the UN resolution on the arms embargo. Now Iran is being threatened by sanctions from the United States, in view of the nuclear programme of Iran's, so I don't see why Iran would not show us documents that we know do exist. So I think we should go on insisting that Iran submits these documents. If we do not receive them by the 15th of February, it would be desirable to have a representative of the Government of Iran present here. I believe that it is also in the interest of Iran to provide these documents to us, because this is, indeed, a drastic violation of Security Council resolutions, and this did affect our situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina. It kept the war going, and it put off a political solution in the country, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My last question regarding the binding-order motions is related to Pakistan, the motion of which was filed on 10th of August, 2009. Mr. Karadzic, yesterday we received your submission notifying us of your withdrawal of this motion. The Chamber, therefore, does not consider that there is any further action it needs to take in relation to Pakistan at this time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do agree, although it would be very useful to have interviews with their general who was head of their secret services. Obviously, we have a problem in that regard, so I decided to withdraw that motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That exhaust my list of pending binding-order motions, and we will take into account what you have said today, and, indeed, hold the hearing on 15th of February, 2010, commencing at 9.00 a.m., to which the representatives of several states, which will, no doubt, include the Government of Germany, will be invited. We will notify you as soon as possible which states will be invited to this hearing. Mr. Tieger, should the Prosecution wish to participate in the hearing, I believe that would be helpful. The only final question I wish to ask, in connection with the binding-order motions, is whether you anticipate filing any further binding-order motions in the coming weeks, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg your pardon. Are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, whether you are planning to file any further binding-order motions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that depends on whether we are going to receive additional material from Bosnia-Herzegovina, because they have a vast amount of material pertaining to investigations of the members of their own military police, and we have objections to their conduct, and we believe that it is of relevance in respect of the conduct of our armed forces, our police, and our civilians. So that is to be expected. As for this letter to the United Nations, perhaps -- I beg your pardon. The United States of America. Perhaps we should write to the United States of America again. At first, they showed goodwill, they really wanted to help us, but then they provided us with material that we didn't actually need, that we weren't really asking for. Turkey, to the best our knowledge, has some important material as well that would be of major significance for these proceedings. We'll see. I believe that we are going to file a binding-order motion as well that EU and the UN should also disclose some documents to us, and I believe that we are going to make certain requests in this respect. As you know, on the 8th of January we filed a 54 bis motion, and we'll see what its fate will be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Given that the binding motions hearing will be mainly of a legal nature, I would strongly recommend that your legal adviser be present at the hearing on 15th of February. Is there anything else that you wish to raise on this general topic before we move to the next item of the agenda for today, i.e., the binding-order motions?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think not, Your Excellency. At this point in time, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I come to, then, the other pending motions. In addition to the binding-order motions, there remain a few other motions pending before the Trial Chamber. There's no need to get into the detail of any of these today, unless either party has specific questions to raise. The Chamber is considering each of these motions carefully, and it is our hope that decisions on some of them will be issued prior to the resumption of the trial proceedings on 1st of March. In particular, the decisions on the two remaining Rule 92 bis motions filed by the Prosecution should be issued prior to the resumption of the trial, possibly also the decisions on the two remaining Rule 92 quater motions filed by the Prosecution. I would hope also the decision on the Prosecution's motion for leave to file a supplemental Rule 65 ter exhibit list. However, much depends on other developments between now and the 1st of March, but I simply wish to inform you that the Chamber is making progress on these and the other pending decisions, and we will do our best to issue them in the coming few weeks. Does either of the parties have any comments to make on this matter? Yes, Madam Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, just one point. You have not mentioned the motion for additional notice of adjudicated facts, Sarajevo, Dragomir Milosevic. It would be definitely helpful to get a decision on this motion as well, because that may lead to the fact that we can withdraw further witnesses from the Sarajevo component of the case. It would be very helpful. I'm aware that it was filed late, and the response is due also on the 15th of February, but perhaps it is still possible. It would be helpful, definitely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We are aware of that situation, and the Judges, as well as all the staff, are working very hard on it. But we're looking forward to the accused's response, which is due on 15th of February, as you indicated. Thank you, Madam Uertz-Retzlaff. Mr. Karadzic, do you have anything to add to this as regards pending motions?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In principle, I notice and I'm afraid that either due to the haste for the closing strategy, I note a tendency for this trial to be transformed into a paper trial. Every effort is being made to reduce to a minimum the appearance of witnesses here. A large number of them are under 92 bis - unfortunately, there are some 20 - and 92 quater, a large number of adjudicated facts, and I wonder how we're going to establish the truth here, not only about my involvement in the events but the events themselves, because I claim that that truth has not been established in any trial so far. It is my duty to inform the trial that for us in the Balkans, and from our own legal system, the differences in legal systems has a terrible effect. We have an investigating judge who co-operates with both parties and who establishes a large number of facts even before an indictment is issued. Here, we have only the one-sided investigation of the Prosecution, and our people simply cannot find their way because of the absence of an investigation. Therefore, my appeal would be to have as few paper documents as possible and to have as many live witnesses so that we can really judge the facts on the basis of investigation that I will undertake if I am given the time and the funds to do it, because otherwise we wouldn't have to appear at all. We could mathematically look through the documents, add up the facts, and pass judgement. And I think this is the last chance for us to make an improvement in that sense. As you know, I'm, in principle, opposed to a paper-ish trial, but the members of my team will do everything in their power to interview as many of the 92 bis witnesses as possible. And as you have seen, we have already done so with some and have provided some additional information. And we will -- for each witness that we interview, we will seek that that witness appears. You will see that there are witnesses who did not appear anywhere. No one examined them, and their statements were built into other trials and now they are to be built into this one, but no one has tested such statements through a cross-examination. And you will see how many witnesses of this kind we have. So this is a completely paper trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, as you'll see in the future, we'll be hearing evidence of witnesses coming to The Hague for more than at least two years from now, and this is far from being a paper trial. In any event, the Chamber will do its utmost to ensure that your trial be a fair one and your rights -- your fundamental rights not be infringed by any means. The next item relates to logistical problems raised by the accused's letter of 15th of January, 2010. In this regard, I'd like to note for the record that Ms. Anna Osure, the acting head of the Office for Legal Aid and Detention Matters in the Registry of the Tribunal, is in the courtroom to answer any questions that the Chamber may have. Thank you, Ms. Osure for coming by. Mr. Karadzic, you raised three issues with the Chamber in a letter sent on 15th January which you say are impeding your ability to continue your trial preparations. Upon receipt of that letter, the Chamber asked the Registry to provide it with a report on the issues raised. That report was sent to you by the Chamber's legal officer on 22nd January, and you were invited to make any further comments you wished in advance of the status conference. You chose not to do so. So can I address the last of these three issues set out in your letter; first, which relates to your ability to access your electronic files when you are in the courtroom. The Registry has informed us that the arrangements have been made for you to access your own files on a network either from the UNDU or from here in the courtroom, and this will be operational by 1st of March. This seems to have resolved that particular issue. Do you have any say on this matter, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, this hasn't been settled, because I was promised in June last year that I would have access to a server, and the memory has already been extended twice because the memory is insufficient. And Lord Bonomy instructed orally that I should receive an external hard drive with a sufficient amount of memory, because otherwise something is always lost or upset when the hard drive is being changed, and it is very difficult to work with it after that. So in June last year, I was promised to have access to a server in my room, and a line has been attached, and a nice gentleman has come to see what the signal is like. And since then, nothing has happened. I was also promised access to the phone because I'm bothering the other people in the cells by my calls. Very well, I limit myself to this issue. We'll come back to the telephone. For me, all this is coming late. I should have had this last year to be able to get insight into this vast amount of material. There's more than two million, and the pages disclosed by the Prosecution consist of two and a half million pages, so you can imagine how difficult it is. I don't have a proper team. I only have two team members that are being paid for. So I think this is a very serious impediment to my working properly and on time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, let us deal with matters one by one. I wonder whether you have before you the memorandum conveyed to you through the Registrar. It enumerates three issues: First, access to telephone; second, computer storage space; and, third, use of files in the courtroom. The issue I raised initially was the third issue, use of files in the courtroom, but my understanding that the matter you raised is related to the second one; i.e., the computer storage space or the size of the memory. So what is your observation in relation to the third matter, which I understand will be resolved by 1st of March.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Excellency. Which is the third question; access?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Use of files in courtrooms. So I can repeat my question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, yes, I understand now. I understand, Your Excellency. If we are talking about use of files in the courtroom, I don't need that before the actual beginning, whenever that beginning is. But regarding the beginning, it would be useful to have it at the beginning, though, of course, I would need a little time to practise. And if I receive payment, I hope I will have someone in the courtroom to assist me in the use of these files in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay. I will come to the second issue raised by you in your letter. I think it is somewhat connected, in that it relates to your ability to store your files electronically, as you indicated. Am I correct in understanding the problem is simply one of memory or the size of memory, and what you are seeking is a way to increase the memory that you have on your computer so that all of your files can be stored and easily accessed? Am I correct in so understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the meantime, I have had two expansions of memory. At this point in time, there may be some reserve memory. What I gathered from OLAD last June was that I would get a server that I would be able to access both from the courtroom and from my room, and that my three confidential advisers would be able to have access to that server while in the Tribunal building, so that we would be able to exchange information. Let me just tell you what kind of problems I am confronting. I can have an adviser here for three days a month. He is paid to stay for only three days. So if no one is present here, for instance, the ICMP material, there were 973 pages, I wanted to send them by e-mail or in some other way. I would have to print it for this to be sent by fax. And for this, it would take three days. And in view of the progress made in technology, I should be able to communicate with my team both by telephone and through the server, but I have learnt that they would not have access to this material. Why not, if they are my advisers and have a confidential status? There's some rules that I simply do not understand. They are highly limiting. We are in a worse position now than in November, when we were discussing the beginning of trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think Judges are that computer literate, so we may need the assistance of Ms. Osure. So could you let us know what the situation is?

utterances.speaker: MS. OSURE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would like to first clarify the information the accused has just informed the Court about, that he was apparently informed by OLAD that he would be -- his legal associates would be able to access the server. Now, unfortunately, this cannot be done, and the reason why we cannot do this is because there are controls in place in the Detention Unit particularly with regard to exchange of digital information, and it's only counsel who represent an accused who can exchange digital information, and they do this by providing the digital information, for example, CDRs, DVDRs, to the management of the Detention Unit, who then pass it on to the accused and back to them again. These controls are in place for a purpose and the security and good order of the Detention Unit, as well as the computer regulations they have to be controlled. Now, we have extended this to legal associates to self-represented accused who are not counsel but are support staff to the self-represented accused, and it's a position of trust and immense responsibility, indeed, but they have been -- I'd say the Registry has granted them this privilege to enable them to be able to conduct the very limited role of consultation with the accused. But now to go to the extent of also allowing them to exchange electronic files with the accused really is beyond anything that we can allow. This means that we will not be able to control any of the movement of digital material between him, meaning the accused, and his Defence support staff. And in addition, we've also -- this is even ground-breaking. We've even provided or are working towards providing him a server in the Detention Unit, of course, which he can access here, which we've gone through all over the world, we've checked examples and seen how this is done, and found that there's no detention facility where this is done. So we've really just reached the limit. This is the most we can do, and, unfortunately, we cannot allow his support staff, just as we cannot allow counsel, to share electronic files in this manner. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sharing the information in this manner, meaning using a server system; is it correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. OSURE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, would you like to make any observation to this?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Excellency. Let me say this: First of all, I am surprised that the confidential relationship between the accused and his associates, even if he's defending himself, I'm surprised that such a confidential relationship has to be controlled. These are three legal advisers who have been nominated here, and they enjoy privileged status. But I am not opposed to the Detention Unit having the password for this server and for them to supervise the information we are exchanging. Of course, I would be opposed if the Prosecution would have insight. But for everyone else, I don't mind whether they have access or not. It is impossible for me to receive 1.500.000 electronic pages without having the electronic ability to exchange this with my associates. We can't be half fish, half maiden. We can't use technological advances only up to a point. Either all million and a half pages will be printed, which is a terrible undertaking and expense, or my advisers with a privileged status should be able to have access to what I have on the server, and vice versa. But I'm not opposed to the Detention Unit or whoever, except for the OTP, whoever wishes to have insight or to control these files, though I believe that between the accused and the privileged members of his Defence team, there shouldn't be any control, because these are professionals and they have obligations towards this Tribunal and towards their profession. So I feel that my hands are tied. I have rights, but not the ability to make use of those rights. So I simply do not understand. Or let us then go back to printing everything, because this kind of limitation due to a lack of confidence -- but as I am saying, I allow everyone to have access to what I am exchanging with my legal associates, except for the OTP, the opposing party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: However, in any event, this is not a proper place to resolve the issue, and we have to leave the matter at that now. So it is mainly for the Registrar to regulate the practice, and only to the extent it affects your right to the fair trial the Chamber will look into the matter. So we advise you to raise, in writing, if you find it necessary, to bring it to the attention of the Chamber. Let me turn to the first issue, i.e., the telephone lines. And I would like to understand how the system currently works and wonder if Ms. Osure again can help us on the number of phones -- the number of phone lines available to Mr. Karadzic, how many other detainees those phone lines are shared with, and what the real assessment of the telephone infrastructure of the UNDU entails. Ms. Osure.

utterances.speaker: MS. OSURE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The accused has access to two telephone lines in his wing in the Detention Unit. There's a privileged line and a monitored line. Now, in addition to this, there is also a privileged line in the office used by self-represented accused, which we continue to encourage him to use, but unfortunately he has not made use of it. Now, if he could make use of the telephone in the office for self-represented accused, that would certainly alleviate some of his concerns. At the moment, I wish to highlight that we are working towards changing the infrastructure of telephone access by detainees, and although we will maintain the same access for the monitored line, this is a much bigger project that will take a lot more time than we anticipated in the beginning. But as an interim measure, we have already contacted the relevant authorities so that we put in place a monitored line in the office used by self-represented accused. And if the accused does use this line, which we hope shall be put in request, as we've requested it as a matter of urgency, so we hope it should be put in place hopefully as soon as the technicians from the relevant company are able to do so, he will certainly be able to have access to this line and share it with the other self-represented accused. Currently, the total number is three. So once again I mention that we encourage him to make use of the facilities in this office, as opposed to using the telephones in the wing shared by all the other accused. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, would you like to make any observation on this?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That would be nice if it were as Ms. Osure has described it, but it is not. I can provide three numbers of my associates, and they are rarely in the office. So I can call on the privileged line only when they're in the office, not on their mobile. Furthermore, I do not have a phone in the office that I should use as a self-represented accused. There is an attachment, but there's no telephone. I don't mind if it were to be monitored, but let me explain how it is in the Detention Unit. There are many breaks when I cannot telephone. There are two walks, one or two sports activities, two breaks for lunch and for dinner, so that during that time I cannot use the phone. For the rest of the time, I share this public telephone with the other detainees. Of course, my needs are greater, because they call their family and lawyers, whereas I call my associates and investigators. So I spend an enormous amount of time on the phone. And luckily we still haven't quarrelled, but this leads to tensions, and it is unnecessary to have such tensions. The privileged line, I can only use the privileged line rarely, because as I have said, my associates are not always in the office. If I were to receive tomorrow a monitored line in the office, as Madam Osure has said, this would solve the problem to a high degree. It's not difficult for me to go to the office and to call from there, and even pay if it is necessary, and there's no problem if it is monitored, but I need to spend an enormous amount of time on the phone. And this would solve it if it were to be in the way Ms. Osure has said, but it is not, if you take into account the breaks, the fact that I cannot reach my associates in their office because they're not there. So I don't have much use of the privileged line. But, Your Excellency, with your permission, I don't need this on the 1st of March or whenever the proceedings begin. I needed this yesterday, the day before, last year, because I am unable to contact my associates. They need instructions from me, and I do not have the ethical power to give them instructions when they were not paid for it. There's some amateurs that are helping me in the preparation of this trial, so I have to communicate with them. And amateurs are, of course, nonprofessionals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I wonder whether Ms. Osure wishes to reply to Mr. Karadzic's comment.

utterances.speaker: MS. OSURE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do not have anything further to add, but I would like to, once again, inform Mr. Karadzic that indeed we're working towards making sure that a monitored line is placed in the office for self-represented accused, and you will be able to share this with the other self-represented accused. But unfortunately we cannot provide you with a telephone to use on your own, as you have requested not just now, but you have frequently requested, because we did undertake a policy decision that this would not be done again after the Parker report in which Judge Parker informed -- or, rather, stated -- concluded that the fact that the former president, Slobodan Milosevic, had a phone of his own, could have compromised security. And on this I refer you to paragraphs 129 of this report and the first lines of paragraph 130. So as a result of a policy decision, we will not be providing telephone lines to any detainee to use on their own in the same fashion. But if you can bear with us, you will be provided -- all self-represented accused will be able to use a monitored line that will be placed in the shared office. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we'll leave the matter there, and I hope this opportunity -- has served as a good opportunity to understand each other. And I advise you to work with the Registry or discuss with them further for the further improvement, if any. And if you find there's an issue that relates to your right to a fair trial, then raise it to the Chamber in writing later on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I, Excellency? I'd like to add something. First of all, I don't think that President Milosevic did something intentionally or consciously with that telephone. Secondly, there's no reason to deny me that. However, I will be pleased if I have a monitored line in the office for work. Whenever I need to, I'll go down to that office and use that line. But the important thing for me is to be able to reach my associates at any point in time, no matter where they are. I also do not mind about the privileged line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I hope that measure could be implemented as soon as possible. Then I turn to my last agenda relating to the resumption of trial on 1st of March in 2010. The Chamber has ordered that the trial will resume on 1st of March, 2010, which is a Monday. We will plan to sit for three days that week, as we indicated earlier on. And for the remainder of March, the Registry has not yet prepared the March court schedule, and as you know, there will be many cases sharing our three courtrooms, so I cannot yet tell you which days or times we will sit. But it remains our hope that we will be able to group together sitting days so that, for example, if we sit on Wednesday, Thursday, and Friday one week, we can sit on the Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday of the following week. This may not always be possible. However, the Registry will do its best to accommodate us. In this regard, I would like to express our deep appreciation for the commendable efforts by the Registry, in particular the CMSS, to enable us to conduct simultaneously nine trials in three courtrooms for March. On a separate note, the Chamber's order on the procedure for the conduct of trial of 8th of October, 2009, sets out the timing of notification of witnesses on a monthly and weekly basis. Indeed, we received notification from the Prosecution in October and November of last year indicating the witnesses it intends to call first at trial. I'm sure that everyone is working on the assumption that those lists remain largely unchanged. Nonetheless, it would be helpful if the Prosecution could file the necessary witness list for March and April so that it is absolutely clear to everyone if there has been any change. According to my reckoning, this would mean that on 1st of February, the Prosecution should file its witness list for March and April, and on April 1st it should file its witness list for May and June, and so on. Similarly, on 20th February or the next working day, the Prosecution should file its monthly list for March which includes a few more details pertaining to exhibits and the time to be taken for examination-in-chief. Mr. Karadzic, you should file by 27th February, or the next working day, your notice of the time you expect to take in cross-examining the Prosecution's listed witnesses for March. On 25th February, the Prosecution will need to file its weekly witness list for the week beginning 1st of March. And on 26th February, Mr. Karadzic should file his notice of his time he expects to need for cross-examination of those witnesses. This issue of witness notification leads us to another issue, which is your opening statement, Mr. Karadzic. In order for the Prosecution to be able to schedule travel for its first witnesses and for you to be able to file the appropriate notification, it needs to know, I imagine, whether you intend to take up two days, the 1st and 2nd of March, for your opening statement. You had indicated previously that you would need the same time as the Prosecution had for its opening statement, and so we are prepared to set aside those two days for that purpose. But if you have decided to defer your opening statement until the start of your Defence case, or if you already know that you will need less than the two days, it would be helpful if you could let us know now. Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Excellency. I'm afraid that the beginning of the trial on the 1st of May [as interpreted] is imperiled by the further deterioration in the conditions that the Defence is facing, but I'll get back to that later. As for the opening statement, I stand by what I have already decided. Two days, a total of six hours, like the other side had, the other party. It would be a good thing if I had more time, but I don't think it will be less. I will do my best to present, during those six hours, everything that I believe is necessary so that the Chamber and the opposing party could hear that at the very outset. That will provide certain directions -- or, rather, a road map, as it were, in terms of the direction in which the Defence will be moving. As for notice of time for cross-examination, of course, if it's the 1st of March, then on the 26th or 27th of February I will be in a position to say so, if I receive information on the 20th of February. However, I have to say in advance that I'm afraid that the greatest problem here is going to be the time given to the Defence. Namely, since there is such a great deal of adjudicated facts and material according to Rules 92 ter and quater, the Defence will need a lot more time than what the Prosecution will use, for example, for 92 quater examination of witnesses. I hope that the Trial Chamber will see how necessary this is for the Defence, of course, provided that we use our time efficiently and rationally. However, it is a fact that time is going to be our greatest enemy once the trial starts, the greatest enemy of the Defence, that is, even more so because the Defence will have to keep investigations going on all the time because of that difference in systems that I already mentioned and that is so disastrous for defendants coming from the Balkans.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So for clarification, then, can I take it that you are, indeed, planning to present your opening statement on 1st of March for two days?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, if you decide that it is going to be the 1st of March after all. However, there is this other point that I wish to speak about; namely, the preparations of the Defence. If you give me the opportunity to do so, I will then present my position. Namely, I will file another motion for postponing the start of trial. It's not that things haven't improved. On the contrary, things have become worse during this break, which was no break at all for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Unless the Prosecution has a matter to raise at this moment, I will hear from the accused on that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, nothing to raise at this moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you indicated you are minded to file a further motion for further postponement, so the Chamber is of the view that you should do so; that is, to file a motion in writing as soon as possible, unless you have a very urgent matter to raise at this time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do, Your Excellency. I cannot file it now in writing until I see what it is that OLAD or, rather, the Registry is providing for me. There are some minor misunderstandings, or, rather, there are certain things that are minor but cause a major effect in terms of Defence preparations. For one, the OLAD believes that the trial has not started yet, whereas the Trial Chamber believes that the trial has started. And OLAD believes that they don't have to pay anything for these three months that have been provided until the 1st of March, because they believe that this is a break. It is not a break for the Defence. It is not only that we have to deal with the previous material, but during this so-called break the Defence received almost 300.000 new pages disclosed by the OTP. That is to say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, if you're going to raise the issues relating to remuneration of your legal advisers and legal associates, I will say there's no point at this time to raise it at the status conference. My understanding is that those matters are before the President, and I hope that those matters will be resolved as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first decision of the President of the Tribunal for the pre-trial phase was a very reasonable one, and we are satisfied with that decision. And in that decision, the President ruled that the position of OLAD was unreasonable. So it really depends on the President's decision, how much postponement I'm going to ask for. Things became worse because 291.000 new pages, to be precise, were disclosed by the OTP in the meantime. I believe that it does pertain to fairness of trial if the Defence has no conditions to prepare, not to go into the question of equality of arms, if they have no arms at all to prepare. When the President's decision is clear, then I will be in a position to see how much time we will need to prepare, because the number of people I will have will depend on that decision. Also, I will have to increase the number of investigators out in the field. It all depends on that, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay. We'll leave it there. So I hope those remuneration matters will be resolved as soon as possible and that --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellency, may I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, I will hear from you first.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was wondering whether this was the right moment for me to file, in writing, a request for the Trial Chamber to provide instructions for translating a book. I have been asked to mark some paragraphs in that book that are needed to be translated, but there's so many that it might as well be the entire book. It is the diary of Professor Nikola Koljevic. From July 1993 onwards, he wrote everything down. He is a participant and a witness. Unfortunately, he passed away. But the book remains with us, and it is an important source of knowledge and information. I was told by the relevant service that it is only the Trial Chamber that can ask for the translation of the entire book. Basically, it does amount to almost the entire book, if I mark all the relevant paragraphs. If the diary of the vice-president of Republika Srpska, who was such an important participant, is not eligible for translation, then I really don't know what else we'd need to translate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We cannot rule on it in a vacuum without understanding what it is about, so I would like you to put into writing and to file a motion, to which the Prosecution may wish to respond, and the Chamber will issue its decision. As to the resumption of trial, I wanted to make you sure that it was the -- it is the Trial Chamber's position that this case was ready for trial as of October or November of last year, and if there's a change of circumstances that warrant further adjournment of the trial, that you should put it into writing again and to file it in a motion. Apart from those things, does either of the parties have any other issues that they wish to raise at this time? Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to raise the question of ICMP material. There is 5.500 something DNA samples. We are in the process of making samples, but we're asking for the entire base to be submitted to us. And the only impediment was the question of confidentiality -- rather, the question of names. It's the families who could challenge that. We are prepared to receive the material without any names, but we cannot make samples until we get the entire database with all the DNA information we need and all the genetic material that we should look into. It is over 300 -- over 300 variables, or, rather -- or, rather, samples. So I'm afraid that this is going to be a major problem, even more so because we have received some information to the effect that this institute that the Prosecution relies on does not have many things that they should have. However, the Defence is going to be very persistent in this regard, that this Court should not act in a way which would not be permissible in any other system. That is to say, this institute should provide genetic material -- rather, all the findings so that we could do what is up to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So in this regard, what we are going to say is -- would be the same; that I would advise you to continue to work with the ICMP, either directly or through the assistance of the Prosecution, to get the material on a voluntary basis, and at the end of the day, if necessary, you file in the way of a motion. Then the Chamber will consider the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If there is nothing further to raise at this moment --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence has nothing, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The hearing is now adjourned until 15th of February.
